ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: The Man Who Painted the Ground

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: A cod fisherman whose crewmates had a whip-round to send him to art school — and who ended up with **5,405 of his works** in the city's collection and a museum on the hill with his name on it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: **Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval (1885–1972)** is one of the **central pioneers of modern Icelandic painting** — that is how the museums put it, and it is the honest framing. "Iceland's greatest painter" is an opinion, however widely held.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: He came to it the hard way, off a fishing boat, and trained in **Copenhagen**. What he did with it was the un-obvious thing: he **got down on the ground**. Icelandic landscape painting had been all mountains and distance; Kjarval knelt over the **moss, the lava and the cracks** and painted the three feet in front of his face.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: In among the rock he painted **faces and figures** — that is real, and it is where the elf stories come from. But be careful with it on the mic: the **fantasy forms appear in parts of his work**, not in every canvas, and **not every odd-shaped rock he painted is a documented hidden person.** The lava is the subject. The faces are the seasoning.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: **Kjarvalsstaðir**, on **Klambratún**, opened in **1973** — the formal opening was **24 March** — and was designed by **Hannes Kr. Davíðsson**. It is **one of the three buildings of Reykjavík Art Museum**, alongside **Hafnarhús** and **Ásmundarsafn**. It carries special responsibility for his work, but it is a general exhibition space too, not a one-man shrine.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: The numbers behind that responsibility are startling. The city's own 2019 operating report lists its registered Kjarval holdings as **5,405 works** — **195 paintings, 5,167 drawings and 43 other pieces** — out of **17,495** works in the whole museum collection. **He is very nearly a third of it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: And the honours story is better than the version you usually hear. He did **not** simply refuse the **Order of the Falcon** out of modesty. An honour proposed in **1965** was **initially declined**, and what followed was a negotiated arrangement, with the insignia ending up associated with the **National Gallery**. A man who said no, then let them find a way round him.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: The Brewery That Outlived Prohibition

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: A brewery founded in **1913** — and **two years later Iceland banned the lot.** It is still here. It outlasted the ban by seventy-four years and then sold the country its Christmas drink.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: **Tómas Tómasson** founded **Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson** in **1913**, and the company's own history dates the first production and delivery to **17 April**. A newspaper from **March 1914** already names him as owner and notes he had worked at the **Sanitas** soft-drink factory — so he learned fizz before he learned beer.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: It is named after the saga poet and warrior **Egill Skallagrímsson**. The company links him to ale; **why Tómas actually picked him is not recorded anywhere I can stand behind**, so anyone who tells you it was because Egill was a famous drinker is guessing.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: **Prohibition did not arrive in one go.** The law was passed on **30 July 1909**; the **import ban** bit on **1 January 1912**; the **general sales ban** on **1 January 1915**. **Wine came back in 1922**, **spirits in January 1935** after a referendum — and **beer stayed illegal until 1 March 1989.** Seventy-four years. A country that allowed you brandy but not lager.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: Here is the part everyone gets wrong: **"pilsner" was never alcohol-free.** Icelandic law set the line at **2.25% ABV** — at or below that, a drink was legally not *áfengi* at all. So the shelves held real, weak beer the whole time. Ölgerðin sold **malt drinks, soft drinks and 2.25% beer** for three generations.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: And there was one loophole with a uniform on. From **1940** Ölgerðin brewed **Polar Ale for the occupying forces**, whose bases sat outside the domestic rules. **Full-strength beer was being made in Reykjavík — Icelanders just were not allowed to buy it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: **1 March 1989**, beer came back, and Icelanders called it **Bjórdagur** — Beer Day. Not an official holiday. Just a nation marking the end of the daftest rule it ever wrote.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: The other legacy is in every fridge at Christmas: **Egils Malt mixed with Appelsín**, the orange fizz. The argument about **which one you pour first** is genuinely national, and there is **no single correct ratio** — anyone insisting on equal parts is stating a preference, not a tradition.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: One modern footnote, because it changed six months ago: in **February 2026** shareholders renamed the listed parent company **Bera hf.** — the Nasdaq Iceland ticker went **OLGERD → BERA on 4 March 2026** — and the drinks business now trades as **Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson ehf.** The brewery is still at **Grjótháls**. Same beer, new letterhead.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: One small river feeds the city, waters it, lit it, and holds the argument about where its parliament began. Most capitals would settle for the water.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: We counted the salmon with a camera, bought the river outright, and got a king to pull the switch. For a stream you could throw a stone across, it has had a career.

ctx: bad-weather alternative — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Weather pivot: "In this you will not see much of the valley — but you are driving over the river that runs the whole city, and that is the point of it."

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Most capitals get a grey, sad little river. Reykjavík's hands you **dinner, drinking water, electricity — and an argument about where parliament started.** Show-off.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Meet the **Elliðaá** — one of very few **capital-city rivers anywhere with a wild Atlantic salmon run.** And I can give you the real count, because they put a **camera counter** in it: in **2009** the whole run was **1,533 fish** — **1,242 through the counter and 291 caught below it** — and the report is explicit that these were **naturally produced salmon, because no smolts had been released the previous year.** In **2003** it was **1,067**. (If you have heard "two and a half thousand salmon", that number is real but it is the wrong animal: **2,500 is a batch of smolts**, not returning adults. I have said it wrong myself.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: The stock has been **monitored continuously since 1988**. It **crashed in 1997**, they moved fish and stocked fry where spawning had failed — and the line that matters is this one: **all stocking has since been stopped, because the run now renews itself.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: The city was so taken with the river it **bought it in 1906**, for hydro power. (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: **The tap water your hotel keeps bragging about starts here too.** **Vatnsveita Reykjavíkur was formally founded on 16 June 1909**; water was taken **straight out of the Elliðaár that summer**, and from **Gvendarbrunnar**, the springs by **Elliðavatn**, later the same year. Two different supplies, same valley — and the Gvendarbrunnar water is the one you are drinking.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: **The lights: Elliðaárstöð, switched on 27 June 1921** — and not metaphorically. **King Christian X and Queen Alexandrine were inside the station and started the first two machines themselves.** It opened as a **1,500-horsepower plant producing 1,000 kW**, and was expanded over the years to about **3,150 kW by 1933.** I will not tell you it was Iceland's second power station or its biggest, because **neither of those rankings survives checking** — plenty of small plants were already running by 1921.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: **Iceland's first was humbler.** In **1904** the Hafnarfjörður carpenter **Jóhannes Reykdal**, with **Halldór Guðmundsson**, wired a **9 kW** generator to his workshop stream and lit **sixteen houses and four street lamps.** Officially the country's first power station. Realistically, a shed with big ideas.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits a cluster of settlement-age ruins the state registers as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður* — the ancient Kjalarnes assembly place. **Whether it actually is is a genuinely open question and always has been.** Six seasons of excavation never settled it; **Adolf Friðriksson's position is that the archaeology does not establish a þing-site at all.** **Ari fróði** put that assembly on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, **fourteen kilometres away**, and nobody has ever closed the gap. And the old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: **The heat, too — and this surprises people.** Reykjavík's hot water did not start with a volcano out in the lava. It started **inside the city**: **low-temperature fields at Laugarnes and here in Elliðaárdalur**, plus **Mosfellsbær** out of town. Those wells still work, and neighbourhoods get deliberately swapped between sources **so the reservoir under the city can rest.** Yes — the ground gets a lie-down.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: Two dead volcanoes, a stack of ice ages, and not one agreed number on the whole thing — and the city still checks it every single morning.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: This is the most looked-at mountain in Iceland and we cannot tell you for certain how old it is or how tall it is. Dark bands warm, pale bands frozen. That part we are sure about.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: That is not a mountain. It is **at least two dead volcanoes wearing one name** — and the honest position is that **nobody can tell you exactly how old it is or exactly how tall the top is.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: **It is not one mountain, and it is certainly not one volcano.** The rock records **more than one extinct central volcano**: an older **Kjalarnes** centre in the west — which some publications call **Viðeyjareldstöðin**, and whether those are one volcano or two is still argued over — and the younger **Stardalur** central volcano in the east, with its own caldera. Volcanism migrated **eastward** across the whole pile. "Esja" is the name of the eroded mountain mass you are looking at. It is not the name of a volcano.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: **The stripes are climate, and you can read them from your seat.** **Dark basalt** flowed in warm, ice-free spells and cooled in peace. **Pale móberg** is lava that picked a fight with a glacier and lost — erupted under ice, shattered, welded into rubble. **Dark means warm. Pale means frozen.** That is the whole code, and it is the one part of this mountain nobody disputes.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: **How many ice ages are stacked in there? Here is the honest answer.** The peer-reviewed survey — **Leó Kristjánsson, Ingvar Birgir Friðleifsson and Norman D. Watkins** — logged a **2,100-metre composite section across Akrafjall, Eyrarfjall and Esja** and read **at least 11, possibly 16 glaciations** in it, plus **at least 13** across western and south-west Iceland between **3.1 and 1.8 million years ago**. But **that count is for the composite, not for Esja on its own** — several of the lower horizons sit in Akrafjall and Eyrarfjall before the section even reaches this mountain. So you are looking at a stack of ice ages. The number everybody quotes belongs to a bigger profile than the thing out the window.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: **How old? Also genuinely disputed.** That composite section is dated **4.2 to 1.8 million years**. Two University of Iceland theses put Esja's oldest rock at **2.8 million years** and the youngest Stardalur rhyolite at **1.8** — but both trace back through the same 1985 account, so that is **one source wearing two hats**. And the actual **potassium–argon measurements** on the upper rhyolite come out at **1.89 ± 0.08**, **1.78 ± 0.04** and **1.85 ± 0.18 million years.** "Exactly 1.8" is a rounded interpretation, not a reading off a machine.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: **The heights are not settled either**, which for the most-looked-at object in Reykjavík is quietly hilarious. **Hábunga** is the name usually given to the true summit at **914 m** — not confirmed against any official survey record I would stand behind. **Þverfellshorn**, the one everybody actually climbs, is usually quoted at **780 m**; the nearest real published measurement is a **weather station at 783 m** *near* Þverfell, which is a different object on a different spot. And the boulder called **Steinn** is a genuinely documented route landmark — a **kennileiti** — but it has **no registered elevation anywhere.** Touch the rock and you have climbed Esja. Nobody checks. Nobody could.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⛰️ Mount Esja
en: **Which is exactly how the city uses it anyway.** Reykjavíkers do not open the weather app. They look out of the window and see whether Esja is still there.

en: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. There was a **Kjalarnesþing** before it, set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: **Ari fróði** wrote the only near-contemporary line about it, around **1122–33**, and it is worth having in full: *"Alþingi var sett at ráði Úlfljóts ok allra landsmanna þar es nú es, **en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi**, þat es **Þorsteinn Ingólfssonr** landnámsmanns … hafði þar ok höfðingjar þeir es at því hurfu."* Before the Alþingi, a þing on Kjalarnes, held by the first settler's son and the chieftains who joined him.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: Notice what Ari does **not** say. He gives no meeting place, describes no structures, does not call it a vorþing, and never says it was Iceland's first. **Jakob Benediktsson** flagged the open question: was it a district assembly, or an embryo of the national one? ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: The ruins are **13.8 km south**, at **Þingnes** on **Elliðavatn** — and that is where **Jónas Hallgrímsson** actually dug, on **21 June 1841**, with four hired labourers. He counted **about twenty ruins** plus a stone circle, opened the biggest, and reasoned that a þing-site this size in this district could hardly be anything but the Kjalarnesþing. ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: The National Museum went back for **six seasons, 1981 to 1986**, under **Guðmundur Ólafsson**. ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: The famous **"judgement ring"** is two circles, not one: an outer ring built **purely of stone**, about **18–20 m overall and 14–15 m inside**, with a smaller **turf** circle nested in it and paving from a different phase inside that. **No entrance was ever found.** Guðmundur allowed it might be a **lögrétta** — and also weighed a livestock pen, which the central position and missing doorway argue against. The archaeology calls them *circular structures* and leaves the function open. **"Dómhringur" is an antiquarian label, not a result.**

en: **There is no radiocarbon date from Þingnes at all** — the 2004 report says plainly that its charcoal was never submitted. At one structure the activity layer lay **3.5 cm** above that ash, and at an assumed **1 mm a year** that works out at the **early 900s** — the report calls that an estimate, and it is. Activity runs from about **900 into the 1200s**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn

en: The **Sturlungaöld** is usually dated from **about 1220 to 1262** — **Sögufélag says 1264**, because the submission to Norway went **district by district** rather than all at once. Iceland's longest and ugliest internal war.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: Power had pooled into a few big clans, above all the **Sturlungar** — the family of the saga-writer **Snorri Sturluson**. Disputes stopped going to the Althing and started going to **swords, fires and assassinations**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **Spring 1238, at Apavatn** — the lake we just passed. **Sturla Sighvatsson summoned Gizur Þorvaldsson**, who came with **forty picked men**. Sturla swore he meant nothing by it, then **had them all seized and disarmed.** A **book** was produced — the saga says *bók*, not Bible — and Gizur swore **to sail abroad and keep faith**. He did neither.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **Five months later, on 21 August 1238, they met at Örlygsstaðir.** Be honest about the numbers, because the tidy version is wrong: **Íslendinga saga gives shifting totals** as forces joined and split — Gizur and **Kolbeinn ungi** with **1,300** at one point, about **1,300** again at Reykjarlaug, then **Brandur arriving with another hundred**, against **four hundred with Sighvatur** and others besides. A modern Icelandic reconstruction puts it at **more than 1,600 against more than 1,200.** It is **often described as the most populous battle ever fought on Icelandic soil** — and I will give you that description, but **nobody has ever demonstrated it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **Sturla's spear has a name and a problem.** **Grásíða** was **large, old, and not very stiff**: he thrust so hard that men went down in front of him, but **the spear kept bending, and he had to put it under his foot to straighten it** between attacks. A family heirloom, failing in real time, in the middle of the worst afternoon of his life.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **How he died is not one blow, and the saga is specific.** **Húnröður Magnússon** stabbed him through the right cheek. **Hjalti Magnússon** through the left cheek and the tongue. **Böðvar kappi** into the throat. **Gizur** then struck a great axe wound **behind the left ear**. **Klængur Bjarnarson** thrust into the wound already in his throat. **Markús Marðarson** stabbed his belly. **The text names no single fatal blow** — so when you hear that Gizur killed him, that is a summary of a queue.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **Snorri Sturluson — the man who wrote down Norse mythology — was killed at Reykholt on the night of 23 September 1241.** King **Hákon** had sent a letter demanding he come to Norway and answer for himself; **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, his own former son-in-law, brought **seventy men**. **Five went down into the cellar**: Markús Marðarson, Símon knútur, Árni beiskur, Þorsteinn Guðinason and Þórarinn Ásgrímsson. **Símon told Árni to strike.** Snorri said **"Eigi skal höggva"** — *do not strike* — **and the saga records that he said it twice.** They struck. (Íslendinga saga, chapter 156.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **The low point was the Burning of Flugumýri, 22 October 1253** — a wedding ambush, the hall fired with the family inside. It is often compared to a certain television wedding; that comparison is a modern one and I will label it as such.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
en: **And the ending is messier than the textbook.** Beginning in **1262** and finished by **1264**, the districts accepted the King of Norway one by one. The document we call **Gamli sáttmáli** records the conditions — but **no original signed 1262 treaty survives.** The manuscript it comes down in, **AM 45 8vo**, is a **damaged law book written in the second half of the sixteenth century**, and Sagnfræðistofnun at the University of Iceland suggests the text is better read as **a homage document, a list of conditions**, than as a treaty between two parties. **Three hundred years of self-government ended, and we cannot produce the paperwork.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

en: The original **Geysir** is first recorded in **1294**, when earthquakes reshaped the field's springs — at its peak it threw water **60–80 m** up. **It is dormant: its last known eruptions were in 2016.** The one you are here for is its cousin **Strokkur** ("the Churn"), **15–20 m** high and occasionally 40 — and its interval is **not** the five minutes everyone quotes. The monitoring study gives an **observed range of 3.7 to 16.4 minutes.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: Geologically this is the **Geysir high-temperature geothermal field, on the eastern margin of Iceland's Western Volcanic Zone** — the literature's own word for it is a **borderline field**. Water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam and comes back up. (I used to say "the Hreppar block" here. The Hreppar **microplate** is real and it is the regional context between the two volcanic zones — but it is not the name of this field.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir
en: **Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, then **June 2000** — and dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades. **It stirred twice more in early 2016**, which is the last anybody has recorded, and the experts were quick to say that did not mean it was back.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: Iceland grows **tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and strawberries** a shade south of the latitude of **Fairbanks, Alaska** — and the heating bill is a hole in the ground.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village; **Friðheimar** is its headline farm, a working greenhouse where you eat lunch **among the vines**, soup ladled three feet from the plant that grew it. And the village is booming — **474 people on 1 January 2026**, up from **321 three years before**. Grow tomatoes, apparently, and people follow.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: The heat comes out of the ground **200 metres away** and arrives in the houses at **about 95°C**. The glass is only **4 mm** thick — you want every scrap of daylight, so you accept the heat loss — and the place therefore drinks roughly **200,000 tonnes of hot water a year**. The source is **Reykholtshver**, an old geyser that still erupts about **every ten minutes** and delivers **14 litres a second at 100°C**, heating the village's houses and glass alike.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: Here's the bit most guides get wrong: **geothermal gives you heat, not light.** At this latitude the sun effectively resigns in November, so the plants run on **grow-lights powered by hydro**, and **CO₂ drawn from natural geothermal steam** is piped in to speed up photosynthesis. Volcano heats it, waterfall lights it, volcano feeds it. Heat **plus** light, never heat alone.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: The hardest-working department is one nobody applies to: about **1,200 bumblebees**, a species brought into Iceland specifically to pollinate greenhouses. Each can work **around 2,000 flowers a day** in good conditions — and it needs to, because there are **25,000 plants** in there, every one of them opening two to four fresh flowers a day. No sick days, no HR complaints, paid entirely in pollen.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: The output is **up to two tonnes of tomatoes a day**, every day of the year. About **5%** come out scratched, undersized or misshapen — those go straight into the kitchen behind you, which is the real reason the soup exists. Even the green ones left on the plants at changeover get used. Nothing is thrown away.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: **Knútur Rafn Ármann** and **Helena Hermundardóttir** bought the place in **1995**: two greenhouses and a big farmhouse nobody had lived in for years, though there had been growing under glass here since **1946**. In **2008** they opened the farm to visitors as a small sideline. Today **tourism is two thirds of the turnover** and the tomatoes are one third, with **110 year-round staff** and another 15–20 in summer. The sideline ate the business.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: They are still building. **17,000 m² of glass**, of which **6,000 m²** has already swapped the old sodium lamps for **LED** — about **half the electricity** — and the rest follows by **2028**. In **2025** they took over **Jarðarberjaland** next door, Iceland's strawberry specialist, and are taking it from **3,600 to 6,000 m²**, lifting it from **60 tonnes of strawberries a year to 100**. Icelandic strawberries are still only **three to four percent** of the market, so there is room to grow.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: None of this is new here. Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouses went up at Reykir in Mosfellssveit in 1924** — three of them in a single spring and summer — and that is the year the whole industry dates from. The **first greenhouse in Biskupstungur came in 1932**, built at Reykholt by the local schoolmaster, **Stefán Sigurðsson**. Down the road, **Espiflöt** has been going since **1948** and now grows flowers only. And the **very first greenhouse in Iceland**, at Sauðárkrókur in the late 1890s, was heated by **fermenting horse manure** — so on balance, the volcano was an upgrade.

en: **Kerið is about 6,500 years old** — that is the figure in its own geological description, and a scientific outreach article puts it at about 6,600. **You may have heard me say five to six thousand. That was wrong and I have stopped saying it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: It is **about 270 m long, 170 m wide and 55 m deep** — deep enough to swallow a seventeen-storey building. The lake in the bottom is **groundwater, 7 to 14 metres deep**, rising and falling with the water table rather than being fed by any stream. It looks turquoise because water absorbs red light first and the floor is dark. And there is life in it: a **2014 paper found ten zooplankton taxa**, mostly rotifers.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: **The walls are red because the iron in the scoria has oxidised** — it is rusting, and it is young enough to still be doing it. Give it a few thousand more years and it will blacken like its neighbours. (I used to name the mineral. **Nobody has actually published a mineral analysis of this crater**, so I have stopped doing that too.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: **How it formed is genuinely argued over, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** Kerið's own geological account says a **scoria cone that collapsed when the magma drained away beneath it** — explicitly not an explosion. A **2024** scientific article says it is probably a **maar**, blown out where magma met groundwater. **Two respectable accounts, opposite mechanisms, same hole in the ground.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: It is the **northernmost crater of the Tjarnarhólar row**, and the **Grímsnes lavas came from twelve separate eruptive centres** covering about **54 km²**. No single big bang — built up in instalments, the way Iceland does most things.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: Short, but enormous in volume — **Iceland's largest spring-fed river**, averaging about **100 m³/s** of lake-clear, gravel-filtered water.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: That single outlet is the whole reason the engineers loved it. Þingvallavatn behaves like an **enormous header tank**: it refuses to flood and it refuses to dry, which makes the Sog **one of the steadiest rivers in the country** — exactly what a turbine wants.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: Three stations sit on it, and they were built a generation apart. **Ljósafossstöð** (1937), **Írafossstöð** (1953) and **Steingrímsstöð** (1959) — together about **88 MW**, which ran roughly **half of Iceland's electricity** through the 1960s and 70s, until the big highland plants on the **Þjórsá** took over.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: **Ljósafoss** opened in **1937** with **two machines of 4.4 MW**; a **third of 5.8 MW** followed in **1944**, taking it to **14.6 MW** — about **105 GWh** a year. Scale was never the point. **Being first was.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: **Írafoss** came online on **16 October 1953** with **two machines of 15.5 MW**. The **third, 16.8 MW, was not added until 1963** — so the famous "48 megawatts" is a *1963* number, not a 1953 one. It harnesses two waterfalls, **Írafoss and Kistufoss**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: **Steingrímsstöð** started up on **6 August 1959**, **26 MW**, and it is the one that dams the **outflow of Þingvallavatn itself**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: And the consequence was entirely domestic. **Ljósafoss quadrupled the electricity available to the capital region**, and **Reykjavík households swapped their coal ranges for electric cookers.** A whole city stopped smelling of smoke because of a drop in a river almost none of them had ever visited.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: Where did Iceland's electric age actually start? Not here — in a **carpenter's workshop in Hafnarfjörður**. On **12 December 1904**, **Jóhannes Reykdal** ran a **9 kW** generator off the stream behind his joinery and lit **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus the workshop and four street lamps**, in time for Christmas. From one carpenter's stream to all of this, inside a single lifetime.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⚡ Sog River
en: **The bill came due in the lake.** Damming **Efra-Sog** in 1959 diverted the water past its own channel and into Steingrímsstöð's tunnels, and the flood thrown up by the construction **swept the spawning gravel out of the Útfall**. The Efra-Sog stock had been **the largest brown-trout population in Þingvallavatn**; as a distinct spawning run, it **disappeared**. The lights went on and a fish went out — and that trade is the honest version of this river's story.

en: Iceland's biggest river spends most of its journey under other people's names and only gets the credit for the last stretch. Which, frankly, is how most job titles work.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá
en: Four rivers walk into a valley. Only one of them comes out with a name — and it is carrying more water than anything else in the country.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá
en: **Ölfusá is Iceland's biggest river by volume.** Orkustofnun's long-run measurements put it at about **400 m³ every second** at Selfoss, averaged over **44 years** — against **363 m³/s** for Þjórsá at Urriðafoss, the runner-up. It is emphatically not the longest. It is simply the one nobody could get across.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá
en: It is **four systems wearing one name.** The glacial **Hvítá** runs south from **Langjökull** past **Gullfoss**, gathering **Tungufljót** and **Brúará** on the way. The spring-fed **Sog** drains **Þingvallavatn** — Iceland's largest natural lake — down through **Álftavatn**. The two trunk rivers meet under the **eastern flank of Ingólfsfjall**, just above Selfoss, and from there they run as one.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá
en: **Veðurstofa Íslands** gauges **5,678 km²** of catchment above its measuring station at Selfoss. Grey glacier-melt and clear spring water, welded into a single channel, with the entire Golden Circle sitting upstream of it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá
en: The channel **zig-zags along the South Iceland Seismic Zone**, following fault lines rather than gravity. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava — erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a fissure **20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, it ran **about 130 km to the sea**, **25 cubic kilometres** of it, reaching the coast between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá. Vísindavefur (Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025) calls it *"stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk"* — the largest lava flow that has run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌊 Ölfusá
en: Keep one distinction straight: **largest by volume is not the same as most powerful.** That trophy goes to **Eldgjá**. The same volcanic system also produced **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477**. (The biggest thing this island ever erupted is shaped like a field. You cannot see it. That is exactly how big it is.)

en: The thing that finally beat this crossing was not an invading army. It was two milk lorries, a tow-rope, and a cable that had been quietly rusting since Queen Victoria.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: A world war could not take this bridge down. The dairy run managed it at two in the morning.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: What is more dangerous to a bridge than a world war? Two milk lorries, one tow-rope, and two o'clock in the morning.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **The town exists because of the bridge.** **Ölfusárbrú** was consecrated on **Tuesday 8 September 1891**, and Vegagerðin's own history records it as **the first suspension bridge built in Iceland** — the first of six of that type raised here between 1891 and 1905. The municipality calls it *"þá mesta mannvirki sem Íslendingar höfðu ráðist í"*, the greatest engineering work Icelanders had ever undertaken. Trade collected at the bridgehead and **Selfoss grew up around it.** The old construction hut, **Tryggvaskáli**, is still the oldest building in town.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **The 1891 numbers.** The Alþingi found **60,000 krónur** — 40,000 as a straight grant, 20,000 as a loan to the counties of Árnes and Rangárvellir, repayable over **45 years**. **Tryggvi Gunnarsson** took the contract because nobody else would do it for that money, and Þjóðólfur reported he lost on the job. The bridge was **built in England** and shipped over ready-made, hung from **three twisted iron cables a side**, painted red, and rated to carry **144,000 pounds**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **Opening day went beautifully right up until they shut it.** Ísafold counted **a full 1,700** people on the riverbank — the largest crowd ever gathered in one place in Iceland outside the capital — and Þjóðólfur reckoned nearer **1,800**, with **just over 1,500** counted walking across in procession behind a brass band. From **just after 11 a.m.** nobody was allowed onto the bridge at all, so the **Governor of Iceland and his entire party had to be rowed across the river** — to attend the opening of the bridge.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **Then at about two in the morning on Wednesday 6 September 1944, the northern main cable snapped.** Two lorries were on the span: a big Dodge carrying **empty milk churns**, towing a second truck that had broken down on the Reykjavík run — both owned by **Kaupfélag Árnesinga**, both on milk haulage for **Mjólkurbú Flóamanna**, the dairy that had been running since December 1929. Both lorries went into the river. **Both drivers lived**; one went under with his truck and surfaced downstream. And get this bit right, because everybody gets it wrong: **the bridge did not fall.** It slumped onto the one surviving cable and hung there, and they used it as a guarded footbridge for another fifteen months.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **It had been warned about, repeatedly.** An engineering inspection that spring produced a **6-tonne limit imposed on 11 May 1944**, repeated on the radio from **29 July**, with bus passengers ordered to get out and walk across. The road director, **Geir Zoëga**, stood on the bank the following afternoon and said only: *"Jæja þá, þá er hún komin svona"* — well then, so that is how it ends. The bridge was **two days short of its 53rd birthday.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **The replacement opened at midday on Friday 21 December 1945, with no ceremony whatsoever.** A suspension bridge with an **84 m main span** plus a 50 m steel-girder approach on the south bank — **134 m in total**, a **6 m carriageway** and a metre of footway each side, the largest bridge in the country at the time. The steel had been trapped behind wartime export bans in America. By the time it opened, the war it was ordered in the middle of had been over for three months.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **The river still rearranges the town.** On **29 May 2008 at 15:45** the ground let go **twice inside about three seconds** — **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, five kilometres north-west of here, and then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault** five kilometres further west again. Veðurstofa announced **6.3** that afternoon, which is the teleseismic figure; the ground-deformation work settles the pair at a composite **Mw 6.1**. Veðurstofa's GPS station at Selfoss **moved about 20 cm to the south-east and rose 5 cm — permanently.** They **closed the bridges over the Ölfusá** as a precaution, which this river has form for. Twenty-eight people were hurt across Árnessýsla; **nobody was killed.** The town shrugged and carried on growing: **11,000 people on 1 January 2026**, up from **9,812** just two years earlier.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏗️ Selfoss
en: **Bridge number three is going up right now.** First sod cut **20 November 2024** — a **cable-stayed** bridge, **330 m long and 19 m wide**, contractor **ÞG Verk**, about **17.9 billion krónur** for the whole scheme, due **autumn 2028**, and reported on schedule as of **March 2026**.

en: Would you move your whole family to an empty island based on where two bits of furniture washed up?

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson
en: That flat-topped mountain is **Ingólfsfjall**, **551 m**, and geologically it is a **móbergsstapi** — a table mountain, built under the ice sheet in the middle of the Ice Age. Hyaloclastite with lava layers running through it, capped by a lava shield from the point where the volcano finally broke out above the meltwater. Its high point is the mound called **Inghóll**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson
en: Per the saga, **Ingólfur Arnarson** threw his carved **high-seat pillars** overboard and swore to settle wherever they washed ashore. His slaves **Vífill and Karli** found them in a bay steaming with hot springs, and he named it **Reykjavík**, "Bay of Smokes."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson
en: **Here is the bit almost everybody gets wrong.** **Landnámabók does not say Ingólfur is buried on that mountain.** The Sturlubók text says only that he spent his **third winter *"undir Ingólfsfelli fyrir vestan Ölfusá"*** — under Ingólfsfell, west of the Ölfusá — before going on to Reykjavík. The burial in Inghóll is **munnmæli**, oral tradition, and the municipality of Ölfus labels it as exactly that on its own page. A 1964 article in **Goðasteinn** called it **þjóðtrú** and said out loud that it doubted it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson
en: The folklore is better than the history anyway. The mound is said to **open for one night every summer**, and on that night you can reach the treasure buried with him. Nobody has produced the treasure. Nobody has produced the grave either.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson
en: **He was not first here, either.** Irish monks — the **Papar** — were already in Iceland and left when the pagans arrived, and a Norseman called **Náttfari** had stayed behind years before. en: Most towns hide their disasters. Hveragerði put theirs in the lobby and charged admission — except for the crack itself, which is free.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: A town of **3,342 people** where the ground occasionally rearranges itself — and the locals responded by **building an exhibition around the crack in their floor**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: Hveragerði sits on its own **high-temperature geothermal field**, at the **eastern margin of the Western Volcanic Zone** and the **western end of the South Iceland Seismic Zone**, with the **Hengill** system away to the north-east. Translation: it is steaming and it is on a fault. Fumaroles and mud pots vent **between the houses**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: **On 29 May 2008 the ground let go twice inside about three seconds.** **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault** five kilometres further west — a doublet. Veðurstofa announced **6.3** that afternoon in Icelandic and **6.1** in its English release, and both are right: **6.3 is the teleseismic estimate, 6.1 is what the ground deformation adds up to.** Hveragerði's GPS station moved **199 ± 4 mm to the north-west**, and kept creeping about **30 mm more** until that August. A University of Iceland study found the damage here **averaged 5% of insured value** and was dominated by **non-structural damage and contents rather than collapse** — which is why the town is still standing and still full.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: **Rather than hide it, they built an exhibition on it.** **Skjálftinn 2008** — "The Quake" — sits inside the **Sunnumörk** shopping centre, over a fissure that runs through the building. And the best part was never meant to be an exhibit: when the centre was under construction in **2003**, an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** Stand on the crack. **Admission is free** — you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator, which runs at over 6.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: **The town has a birthday, and it is younger than your grandmother.** It began in **1929** on land of the farm **Vorsabær** in Ölfus: that summer the milk station went up at **Breiðumörk 26**, and the first two houses appeared — **Varmahlíð**, and a summer house at **Fagrihvammur** where **ylrækt**, growing under glass on geothermal heat, started here. A milk station, two dwellings and a greenhouse. That is the entire origin.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: **Commercial horticulture began the same year, 1929**, associated with **Sigurður Sigurðsson**; a **45 m² greenhouse went up at Fagrihvammur in 1930** for cucumbers and tomatoes. The **Garðyrkjuskóli ríkisins** at **Reykir** — the state horticultural college — turned out **its first qualified horticulturists in the spring of 1941**, and most of them walked straight out and built nurseries of their own here. The count tells it better than any adjective: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flowers took over in the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: **And yes, the bananas.** The horticultural college grew them **as an experiment**, never commercially, and the "Europe's largest banana plantation" line you may have read is a myth with excellent legs. Iceland is not, and never was, a banana republic.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **3,342 on 1 January 2026** (Hagstofa Íslands). The **name** is far older than the town: **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: Uphill behind the town is **Reykjadalur**, registered by **Náttúrufræðistofnun** as a **high-temperature geothermal area** and described by **Umhverfisstofnun** as a landscape of hot springs, pools, dykes, faults and landslides. It is the valley people walk up to sit in a warm river. Note the two are different places: the **geothermal park is in town**, Reykjadalur is the walk.

en: It makes the power, heats half the capital, and files its own exhaust underground as gravel. It also taught Iceland that you can trigger earthquakes by being tidy.

en: Most power stations bury their emissions in a report. This one buries them in the rock.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Those white plumes are **steam, not smoke** — and the same plant that lights the road also **turns its own exhaust into stone**. Underneath you, permanently.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: **Hengill** is not a mountain, it is a **volcanic system** — and it sits where **three zones meet**: the **Reykjanes rift**, the **Western Volcanic Zone** and the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**. Water goes down, comes back at **reservoir temperatures of 260–320°C**, and spins turbines.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: **303 megawatts of electricity**, and the arithmetic is satisfying: **six high-pressure turbines of 45 MW plus one low-pressure turbine of 33 MW.** They arrived in stages — **two in 2006, one in 2007, two in 2008, two more in 2011** — so the plant you are looking at was assembled over five years, like flat-pack furniture for a country.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Then the quieter half. **200 MW of heat** goes **27 km down insulated pipes** to warm **more than half the capital region**, which is why Reykjavík never smells of coal. Nationally, **about 90% of the energy used to heat Icelandic homes is geothermal** — Orkustofnun's figure for **2020**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: The trick that makes it safe: the geothermal fluid down there is **hot, corrosive and full of dissolved minerals**, and **it never touches your tap.** It gives up its heat through an exchanger to clean water, and goes back underground.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: **Carbfix** is the famous bit, and the famous number needs its footnote. In **2012** a pilot dissolved **175 tonnes of CO₂ in 5,000 tonnes of water** and pumped it in at about **500 m and 35°C**. **Matter et al. (2016)** tracked it: **over 95% turned to carbonate rock in under two years.** That result belongs to *that* pilot — **not automatically to every tonne since**, at different depths, temperatures and rock.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Industrial injection is a different animal: it started on **23 June 2014**, putting the plant's own CO₂ **and H₂S** into fractured basalt at roughly **750 m and over 250°C**. By the end of **2017** that had taken down **23,200 tonnes of CO₂ and 11,800 tonnes of H₂S**. *(The line that "both gases mineralise in about two years" mixes two separate studies — do not say it.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: And the newest chapter is barely a year old. **ON Power opened a second capture station, Steingerður, on 19 June 2025** — about **30,000 tonnes of CO₂ a year**. Over the twelve months to **30 June 2026** Carbfix reported **99.6% of the CO₂ and 100% of the H₂S** entering the capture system being dissolved, and **cumulative mineralisation past 120,000 tonnes of CO₂ and 50,000 of H₂S**. *(Operator figures — impressive, and only one source, so say who said it.)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Why bother with the sulphur at all? Because **H₂S stinks and is toxic**, and after the plant opened in 2006 the smell started reaching **Reykjavík** on the wrong wind — around **13,000 tonnes a year** by 2011. Iceland wrote an **ambient H₂S limit in 2010, biting in 2014**, and the cleanup followed. The rotten-egg problem is the reason the rock-making began.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Separately from all that: **Climeworks** pulls CO₂ **out of the open air** here — not out of the turbines. **Orca** started on **8 September 2021** at a nominal **4,000 tonnes a year**; **Mammoth** is nominally **36,000**. Hellisheiði supplies the power, Carbfix supplies the basalt.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: **And it is not free.** When large-scale reinjection began at **Húsmúli on 1 September 2011** at about **500 kg a second**, the ground answered immediately: **two magnitude-4 earthquakes on 15 October 2011**, around **forty events above ML 2.5**, eight between **3.0 and 4.0** — felt in **Hveragerði**, the biggest felt in **Reykjavík** — and up to **2 cm** of measured surface movement. Pushing water into a fault system moves faults. That is the honest footnote to the clean-energy story.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun
en: **The lava out the window has three names, and two of them are the same name.** Properly it is **Svínahraunsbruni** — two historical **ʻaʻā** flows out of the **Eldborgir just west of Lambafell**. In daily speech it is called **Svínahraun**, and so is the much older **Leitahraun** underneath it, which it ran straight over. One of those two flows is the one called **Kristnitökuhraun**, the Christianity Lava. Iceland names a thing twice and then argues about it. Entirely on brand.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun
en: It ran **around the year 1000** — Vísindavefur allows **possibly 999** — covered roughly **15 km²**, flowed **north-east** across the flats into **Þrengslin**, and **stopped about where the Ring Road runs now.** You are driving along its edge.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun
en: **Now the story, with the actual words, because this one gets told wrong everywhere.** Iceland's chieftains were at **Þingvellir**, and the two sides had just formally declared themselves **out of each other's laws** — which, in a country with one legal system and no army, is how a civil war starts.
